facts.statement: The genus Cnemiornis was described by Richard Owen in 1866.
The genus Cnemiornis contains two species: C. gracilis and C. calcitrans.
Cnemiornis is a genus of flightless geese endemic to New Zealand with two species.
facts.quote: The genus, endemic to New Zealand, consists of two species: the North Island goose (Cnemiornis gracilis) and the South Island goose (Cnemiornis calcitrans).

facts.statement: The New Zealand geese were as large as some small moa.
facts.quote: This goose was as large as some small moa.

facts.statement: The North Island species weighed 15 kg and the South Island species reached 18 kg.
facts.quote: The North Island species had 15 kg in body mass while the South Island species reached 18 kg

facts.statement: These geese were flightless and had much-reduced webbing on their feet.
facts.quote: They were flightless, with much-reduced webbing on the feet

facts.statement: The fossil range of Cnemiornis extends from the Otiran to the Holocene.
Cnemiornis lived from the Calabrian to the Holocene, between 1.63 and 0 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Calabrian to Holocene (1.63 to 0 million years ago)

facts.statement: The Māori name for the North Island goose (C. gracilis) was tarepo.
facts.quote: The Māori name of the North Island goose (C. gracilis) was "tarepo".

facts.statement: These geese were never particularly common and faced hunting pressures from settling Polynesians.
facts.quote: They were never particularly common, and like many other large New Zealand endemic species they were subject to hunting pressures from the settling Polynesians

facts.statement: Their eggs and hatchlings were preyed upon by the Polynesian rat and settlers' dogs.
facts.quote: as well as predation upon their eggs and hatchlings by kiore, or the Polynesian rat (which accompanied the settlers) and the settlers' dogs

facts.statement: The parent group of Cnemiornis is the family Anatidae.
Cnemiornis belongs to the family Anatidae.
